tagline: Art, revolution, and a thousand cheeses
overview:
France is the largest country in Western Europe, a six-sided land the French call the Hexagon, about the size of Texas. It has coasts on the Atlantic Ocean, the English Channel, and the Mediterranean Sea, and borders with eight countries, including Spain across the Pyrenees and Italy and Switzerland across the Alps. The capital, Paris, on the Seine River, is one of the most visited cities on Earth, home to the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre museum, and Notre-Dame cathedral. France also includes overseas regions such as French Guiana in South America and islands in the Caribbean, Indian Ocean, and Pacific.

About 68 million people live in France and speak French, a language spoken by hundreds of millions more around the world. France is a republic with a directly elected president and a parliament, and it is a founding member of the European Union. It is the world's most popular tourist destination, a leader in fashion, food, film, aviation, and high-speed trains, and a country where the ideas of liberty, equality, and fraternity, born in its revolution, still shape daily life.
landAndNature: France has almost every kind of European landscape. The Alps rise in the southeast to Mont Blanc, at 4,808 meters the highest mountain in Western Europe, while the Pyrenees wall off Spain in the south. The Massif Central is a plateau of extinct volcanoes and deep gorges. Great rivers, the Loire, Seine, Rhône, and Garonne, cross plains of wheat, sunflowers, and vineyards. The coasts range from the white chalk cliffs of Normandy and the rocky coves of Brittany to the pine-backed dunes of the Atlantic, including the Dune of Pilat, Europe's tallest sand dune, and the sunny Riviera on the Mediterranean. In the marshy Camargue delta of the Rhône, wild white horses and pink flamingos share the lagoons. Wolves and brown bears have returned to the mountains, and ibex leap across alpine cliffs.
peopleAndCulture: French meals are an art: crusty baguettes, croissants, hundreds of cheeses, and dishes like boeuf bourguignon and ratatouille, eaten slowly at long tables. The lunch break is sacred, and the French meal is on UNESCO's heritage list. Paris fashion houses set global styles, and French painters such as Monet and Renoir invented Impressionism. Cinema was born here with the Lumière brothers, and the Cannes Film Festival remains the world's most glamorous. The Tour de France bicycle race is watched by millions each July, and France has won the soccer World Cup twice, in 1998 and 2018. Rugby, judo, and handball are also loved. Comic books, or bandes dessinées, like Asterix are taken seriously as literature. Bastille Day on July 14 brings parades and fireworks.
history: Prehistoric artists painted the caves of Lascaux about 17,000 years ago. Celtic Gauls were conquered by Julius Caesar in the 50s BC, and after Rome fell, the Franks under Charlemagne built a vast empire around 800. French kings ruled for a thousand years, building castles, cathedrals, and the palace of Versailles, and fighting England in the Hundred Years' War, when Joan of Arc became a hero. In 1789 the French Revolution overthrew the monarchy and declared the rights of man; Napoleon then conquered much of Europe before his defeat in 1815. France built a large colonial empire in Africa and Asia. It suffered terribly in World War I and was occupied by Nazi Germany from 1940 to 1944. After the war France helped create the European Union, and its colonies gained independence, often after painful wars.
funFacts: The Eiffel Tower was meant to be torn down after 20 years but was saved because it was useful as a radio antenna.
France has more time zones than any other country, twelve, because of its territories scattered around the globe.
The Louvre is the most visited museum in the world, and walking past every artwork would take months.
French law once required bakers to take vacations in shifts so Paris would never run out of bread.
The metric system, now used by nearly every country on Earth, was created during the French Revolution.
